title: Isolated queen's pawn: pieces on or pieces off
outcomes: Recognises the app's isolated queen's pawn (an isolated pawn on the d-file) and names the blockade square in front of it
States the usual plan for each side as a rule of thumb: the owner keeps pieces on and attacks, the other side trades pieces and blockades
Sees in one worked pair that the engine's verdict can change a lot when pieces come off and whose move it is, and that one pair is not a rule
Chooses a blockade or declines it in positions where nobody names the plan

steps.text: An **isolated queen's pawn** (IQP) in this app is a pawn on the d-file with no friendly pawn on the c- or e-file. No pawn can defend it, and the square in front of it suits an enemy piece. In return its owner gets space and open lines. Rule of thumb: the owner keeps pieces on and attacks; the other side trades pieces and blockades.

**Rule of thumb, with conditions.** The owner's attack tends to work while pieces are still on and the opponent has not pulled back the defenders. Trading pieces can make the pawn harder to defend; one example below shows the verdict moving; it does not show why. A blockade must also be safe: check the square. The next pair of positions differs mainly in the trades, and in the rook placement too. One pair is an example, not a proof.

steps.title: Pieces on, pieces off
steps.prompt: Black is to move in all three; predict where the engine puts each position. In the second, both queens and one rook of each side are gone, and Black's remaining rook stands on the open c-file; the side to move also matters here. The third has no isolated pawn at all. For blockading a passed pawn, see the lesson 'Blockading a passed pawn: check the square'.
In the last two positions, did you blockade? What did you check about the blockade square before you chose or declined?
